title: Range-Based For Loops
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and core rule of range-based for loops using at least one example.
Trace or adapt a minimal C++ example related to range-based for loops and state its expected result.
Identify one precondition, error case, lifetime issue, portability assumption or version constraint relevant to the topic.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text:
Control flow selects paths and repeats work. A reliable loop has a clear invariant, an intentional update and a termination condition that can be tested.

Range-Based For Loops focuses on the decisions and observable behavior named by the subtopics below. The aim is to explain the rule, predict what a small program should do, and then confirm the result with a focused check.

Try a normal input, a boundary input and an invalid input; verify that the program terminates and does not skip required cases.

content_blocks.title: Minimal example: Range-Based For Loops
content_blocks.run_instructions: Save as `example.cpp`. Compile using `g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic example.cpp -o example; then run ./example (Windows: .\example.exe).` The CodeLeaf page shows reference output only; it does not execute C++ learner code.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the example, rebuild with the same standard and warning flags, and rerun the same input. If the example is nondeterministic or depends on platform support, record that constraint instead of expecting byte-for-byte identical output.
content_blocks.limitations: The built-in CodeLeaf page does not execute C++ in a sandbox. Compile local teaching examples only; arbitrary learner code requires a separately deployed isolated runner with CPU, memory, process, filesystem and network limits.
content_blocks.explanation: A range-based for visits each element in the sequence. Use const references when values are large and copying is unnecessary.

items.title: Basic Range-Based Loops
items.text: Explain basic range-based loops in the context of Range-Based For Loops: identify the rule, trace a minimal example, and check one boundary or failure case.

items.title: Iterating Over Arrays
items.text: An array stores a sequence of elements and indexing starts at zero; built-in array bounds are not checked automatically.

items.title: Iterating Over Standard Containers
items.text: Explain iterating over standard containers with its language-standard context and verify implementation support rather than assuming every compiler behaves identically.

items.title: Using References to Avoid Copies
items.text: A reference aliases an existing object and must not outlive that object; references are not reseatable after initialization.

items.title: Using const auto&
items.text: Apply const auto& with explicit preconditions, clear naming and a small test for an ordinary and boundary case.

items.title: Structured Bindings in Range Loops
items.text: A struct groups related data under one type; in C++, its default member access is public, unlike class.

content_blocks.title: Guided practice
content_blocks.text: Before changing the example, predict the output and name the rule that produces it. Then modify one line to demonstrate basic range-based loops, and add a test for one boundary or failure scenario. Keep the experiment small enough that another learner can reproduce it.

content_blocks.title: Version, safety and portability note
content_blocks.text: Use standard C++ rather than compiler-specific behavior unless the lesson explicitly labels the dependency. Feature support varies by compiler version and standard-library implementation. Check the references and prefer explicit diagnostics to assumptions.

content.task: Create a small, independent example that demonstrates range-based for loops. Predict the result before compiling, write down a precondition, and test one ordinary case plus one boundary or failure case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example builds under a documented standard mode with warnings enabled.
The predicted and observed result are recorded; deviations are explained.
At least one boundary, invalid-input, lifetime or portability assumption is tested or documented.
hints: Start with the smallest example that demonstrates basic range-based loops.
Trace the relevant values and state the expected output before running the program.
Check the standard/compiler reference and add an edge case instead of relying only on the happy path.

Keep the important preconditions and trade-offs visible when applying range-based for loops.
Use explicit build settings and focused tests to support the claim that the example behaves as expected.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming one successful example proves every case.
common_mistakes.why: It may miss an invalid input, boundary, error path or implementation difference.
common_mistakes.fix: Write down the preconditions and test at least one ordinary case plus an edge or failure case.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a language feature without checking its requirements.
common_mistakes.why: The code may depend on a standard version, an object lifetime or an API precondition.
common_mistakes.fix: Use the explicit standard mode and verify the relevant rule and compiler/library support.

common_mistakes.problem: Ignoring compiler diagnostics or simplifying away ownership and error behavior.
common_mistakes.why: Warnings and explicit contracts often expose a defect before it becomes a runtime problem.
common_mistakes.fix: Compile with warnings, keep the smallest reproducible sample and state what happens when an operation fails.
